title: HW02-P2 Adv Data Viz
text:
Instructions
Task: Open up the New York Times article A Summer of Strikes, and scroll down to the plot titled “Union membership has fallen sharply over the past four decades (Share of the work force in a union, by industry)”.
Using ggplot2 and other tools in R, recreate this plot. Note that you will need to create the data underlying the plot yourself. You can create this data in R with tibble(). You can also write the data in Excel or Google Sheets and export it as a CSV file.
Requirements:
Bonus: Additional possibilities to enhance your visualization include adjusting the default aesthetics of the arrows, aligning your plots neatly, and adding margins in order to left-align the y-axis text.

title: HW02-P2 Adv Data Viz
text:
Overall

Panels for “All workers”, “By Sector”, and “By Industry” are shown.
Arrows showing the change from 1983 to 2022 are shown.

Note: be sure that the arrows all point in the correct direction!


The actual percentages in 1983 and 2022 are shown as text.
X-axis tick marks are at 0, 25, and 50.
Plot title says “Union membership has fallen sharply over the past four decades”.
Plot subtitle says “Share of the work force in a union, by industry”.


Resource reflection

At least 1 resource is listed
At least 3 sentences about resources and their helpfulness in the task

title: HW02-P2 Adv Data Viz
text:
Setup

Codelibrary(tidyverse)



Codeunion <- tibble(
  group = c("", rep("BY SECTOR", 2), rep("BY INDUSTRY", 10)),
  category = c(
    "All workers",
    "Private sector", "Public sector",
    "Transportation and utilities", "Manufacturing", "Mining",
    "Construction", "Education and health",
    "Arts, entertainment and recreation", "Business services",
    "Retail, food and hospitality", "Public administration", "Agriculture"
  ),
  share_1983 = c(20, 17, 37, 47, 28, 27, 28, 26, 17, 10, 8, 30, 4),
  share_2022 = c(10,  6, 33, 16,  8,  7, 13, 17,  7,  3, 3, 28, 5)
) |>
  mutate(
    group    = fct_inorder(group),
    category = fct_rev(fct_inorder(category)),   
    dir      = sign(share_2022 - share_1983)     
  )

title: HW02-P2 Adv Data Viz
text:
Visualization

Codeggplot(union, aes(y = category)) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = share_1983, xend = share_2022, yend = category),
    color = "navyblue", linewidth = 1,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "in"), type = "open")
  ) +
  # 1983 label sits beyond the tail, 2022 label beyond the arrowhead
  geom_text(aes(x = share_1983 - dir * 2.2, label = share_1983), fontface = "bold") +
  geom_text(aes(x = share_2022 + dir * 2.2, label = share_2022), fontface = "bold") +
  facet_grid(group ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 25, 50)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 50), clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title    = "Union membership has fallen sharply over the past four decades",
    subtitle = "Share of the work force in a union, by industry",
    caption  = "Source: Current Population Survey, via unionstats.com",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
   theme_minimal() +
   theme(
     plot.title.position = "plot",
    strip.text.y        = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0, face = "plain"),
    axis.text.y         = element_text(hjust = 0)
  )

section: 0 Request U.S. Census Data API Key
text:
0 Request U.S. Census Data API Key
In order to retrieve data from the U.S. Census website, and API key is required. Follow the steps below to obtain yours and use it in this homework:

Go to https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html and request an API key.
Save the received key into a file along side this file with the name census_api_key.txt–make sure that the file contains nothing other than the key.
Open GitHub Desktop -> right click census_api_key.txt and select Ignore file (add to .gitignore) to avoid exposing your key to others

title: HW03-P1 Adv Map Viz
text:
1 Load One More Variable
The following code loads census data for Ramsey counties and reads in the pedestrian/bike crash data. Adjust this code to load in one additional census variable that you think might serve as useful context for crash data. To do this:

Look at the documentation for get_acs() by entering ?tidycensus::get_acs in the Console.
Look at the Searching for variables documentation from the tidycensus package. Use the function in this documentation to find one variable to add to the variables argument in the get_acs() function below.
Rename the variable that you picked to have a more descriptive name within rename().


Enter the new variable you selected (e.g., B01003_001) here: ____
Enter the new name for that variable (e.g., population) here: ____


Codelibrary(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidycensus)
library(readr )
library(ggplot2)



Codecensus2020 <- tidycensus::get_acs(
    year = 2020,
    state = "MN",
    geography = "tract",
    variables = c("B01003_001", "B19013_001", "B23006_023", "B25058_001", "B25107_001", "B25003_001", "B25003_002", "B25003_003", "B25077_001", "B08201_002"),
    output = "wide",
    geometry = TRUE,
    key = readLines("census_api_key.txt")

) |>
    filter(word(NAME, 4) %in% c("Ramsey")) |>
    mutate(
        tract = word(NAME, 3),
        tract = str_remove(tract, ","),
        county = word(NAME, 4)
    ) |>
    select(-NAME) |>
    rename(
        "population" = "B01003_001E",
        "medianIncome" = "B19013_001E",
        "bachelors" = "B23006_023E",
        "medContractRent" = "B25058_001E",
        "tenureTotal" = "B25003_001E",
        "tenureOwned" = "B25003_002E",
        "tenureRented" = "B25003_003E",
        "medianHomeValue"= "B25077_001E",
        "noVehicleHouseholds" = "B08201_002E"
    ) |>
    select(-contains("_"))

crashes <- read_csv("https://mac-stat.github.io/data/Crash.csv") |>
    filter(!is.na(Latitude), !is.na(Longitude))

text:
8 Pedestrian/Bike Crashes per Census Tract
Create a map that shows the number of pedestrian/bike crashes per census tract. Write one sentence about the patterns you notices; interpret your findings in the data context.

Use scale_fill_gradientn() to set up a meaningful color scale for the census tract colors.
Include a map layer for the roads.


Codeggplot()  +
    geom_sf(data = roads_sub1, fill = "NA") +
    geom_sf(data = crashes_per_tract_geo, aes(fill = n)) + scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightblue", high = 'red') +

title: HW03-P2 Adv Map Viz
text:
4 Join Walkability & Boundaries
Use st_join() within the sf package to insert walkability information into the all_us_counties dataset. Because the walkability information is available over regions that are smaller than counties, this join will merge in multiple regions of walkability information for each county.
After the join, summarize the walkability index within each county with the weighted mean and weighted standard deviation, where the weights are given by the Shape_Area variable.
Background information about weighted summary measures: In an ordinary (unweighted) mean and standard deviation, each observation gets a weight of 1–that is, every observation contributes equally to the calculation. We want to compute a weighted measure because the regions within a county have different areas.
Techinical implementation: You can install the Hmisc package and use the following:

Hmisc::wtd.mean(x, weights)

Hmisc::wtd.var(x, weights)

This computes a weighted variance–you’ll need to take the square root after this.



Note: DON’T add library(Hmisc) to your package loading code chunk. Hmisc contains a function called summarize() that will conflict with dplyr::summarize().
In both functions, x represents the vector of numerical entries you want to summarize, and weights is a vector of the same length as x that gives the weight for each entry of x.

Code# Use st_join to merge county boundaries and regions where we have walkability index data
all_us_counties_walk_index <- st_join(all_us_counties, walk_index_mn)

# Use Hmisc::wtd.mean() and Hmisc::wtd.var() to compute the weighted mean and SD of the walkability index (weighted by Shape_Area)
all_us_counties_walk_index_summ <- all_us_counties_walk_index %>%
  group_by(COUNTYFP) %>%
  summarise(wtd_mean = Hmisc::wtd.mean(NatWalkInd, Shape_Area), wtd_var = Hmisc::wtd.var(NatWalkInd, Shape_Area) )



Codeall_us_counties_wi_summ_us_state <- all_us_counties_walk_index %>%
  group_by( STATEFP) %>%
  summarise(wtd_mean = Hmisc::wtd.mean(NatWalkInd, Shape_Area), wtd_var = Hmisc::wtd.var(NatWalkInd, Shape_Area) )

Codemn <- all_us_counties %>%
  filter(state_name == "Minnesota")

ggplot() + geom_sf(data = mn) + geom_sf( data = all_us_counties_walk_index_summ, aes(fill = wtd_mean)) + scale_fill_gradient(low = "darkblue", high = "lightblue")

title: HW03-P2 Adv Map Viz
text:
6 Walkability Variability vs Average
Make plots (not maps) that allow you to explore if there is a relationship between the variability in walkability in a county and the average level of walkability in a county. One plot should depict the United States as a whole, and a second plot should break down this relationship across states. Summarize your findings and what you would be curious to explore next based on your explorations.

Looking at counties nationwide, places with a higher average walkability score also tend to show a wider spread in scores, so the two measures rise together. A likely reason is that walkable counties combine dense, pedestrian-friendly urban centers with car-oriented suburbs or rural stretches, which pushes their internal variation up. Counties with low average walkability, by contrast, are fairly uniform, with both the mean and the spread staying low. Minnesota follows the same pattern: urban counties score higher on average and differ more from one neighborhood to the next, while rural counties sit at low averages with little variation. Overall, walkability is unevenly spread inside counties, and urban cores raise both the typical score and the gaps within a county. I’d like to dig deeper into how urbanization, county size, and socioeconomic characteristics shape these patterns from state to state.
